Magnus Effect Powered Drone

Project Overview

The Magnus Ultralight project is an investigation into the experimental aircraft concept of human-scale flight using the Magnus Effect. The goal is to determine the feasibility of and to develop a person-sized eVTOL aircraft that uses a large spinning body to generate lift, capable of efficiently carrying a person large distances. The project began with an investigation into the Magnus Effect as a method for keeping an unmanned small scale quadcopter in the air. Refinements continue to be made to the scale vehicle in order to validate and quantify the effectiveness of the Magnus Effect as a lift generating method. The project will continue with the development of a full scale aircraft, assuming the small scale program is successful. The development of the project is documented below.

Prototype 1

Overview and Results

The initial prototype of the scale Magnus Effect powered aircraft featured a standard quadcopter configuration for vertical takeoff, landing, and forward propulsion, along with two spinning spheres for Magnus Effect lift generation. This prototype was designed by me during the Spring 2025 semester and tested by me and my team during the Summer of 2025. Initial testing of the quadcopter’s airworthiness and the sphere actuation system were hugely successful. However, integrated testing of the full system revealed flaws in the overall design. In order to solve the main issue of the vehicle being too heavy for the VTOL propulsion system, improvements were made throughout the summer to reduce the weight of the vehicle and increase the thrust generated by the propellers. However, through iterative testing, we determined that it was not possible to squeeze enough performance out of a quadcopter of our scale to controllably lift the sphere actuation mechanisms. Although prototype 1 has been shelved in favor of prototype 2, several of its components are being used in the new prototype and a lot was learned about how to develop this novel type of flying vehicle. Iterative improvements

Throughout the fabrication and testing phase of the first prototype in summer 2025, several improvements were made to the design, many of which are carried over to prototype 2. They will be discussed here.

Sphere Actuation Mechanism

Further research and modeling into the drag characteristics of spinning bodies showed that the initial design for actuating the spheres would not be powerful enough to overcome the skin friction drag generated by the 24 in diameter spinning spheres. Given the high Reynolds number of the flow around a spinning sphere, the turbulent boundary layer model of skin friction drag was appropriate. Therefore, the torque necessary to spin each sphere scales by roughly the rotation rate raised to the fifth power. This necessitated more powerful motors than initially thought. However, finding motors that were both reasonably lightweight and powerful enough proved to be difficult, so gearboxes were used instead to gear down high speed lightweight motors.

Insert image here

Additionally, several methods for holding onto the spheres were tested over the course of the summer. This proved to be quite the challenge due to the tendency of the spinning sphere to bend away from its axis of rotation due to the centrifugal force generated. The final design involved a 3d printed hub with six spokes extending from it radially like a cone. The spokes were affixed to an inflated beach ball using epoxy, and provided enough stiffness to keep the ball spinning properly.
